screens.title: Capstone Project: Smart Plant Monitoring System
screens.narratorSegment: This capstone brief frames a practical, end-to-end project: a Smart Plant Monitoring System. You will plan and assemble sensors that measure soil moisture, light, and temperature, present their readings on a small I2C display, and create alerts when the plant needs attention. The project is deliberately modular. That means you first validate each sensor, then integrate the display, then add alerts and calibration, and finally optionally add a relay-driven pump. In practice, this structure helps isolate problems and keeps your code organized. A clear wiring diagram and a README are required for assessment, so document as you go. Throughout, use non-blocking timing with the millis function so your device remains responsive while updating sensors and alarms. Think of this capstone as a demonstration of skills from earlier modules: wiring, analog reading, I2C, conditional logic, debouncing ideas, and safe actuator control. As you build, record a short overview video walking through your block diagram, wiring, expected code structure, and grading criteria. That video tells the story of your design choices. Before you start, ask: which part will you test first, and how will you verify reliable sensor readings?

Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Capstone Brief
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Smart Plant Monitoring System

A modular capstone: sense soil moisture, light, and temperature; display values; alert when conditions need attention; optionally water automatically.

Why this matters
You will combine sensing, display, and control into a reliable, documented device that demonstrates applied embedded skills.
How you'll work
Test sensors first, then integrate display and alerts, then add calibration and optional pump control.
Explore Key Topics
Sensors & Tests
Verify each sensor on Serial before integration.
Display & UI
Format clear labels and avoid flicker using I2C or OLED buffering.
Alerts & Control
Use thresholds, calibration, and non-blocking timing for reliable alerts or pump activation.
Visual concept
Cards represent sensors, display, calibration, and optional pump. Connect them in sequence for a clear build plan.
Soil moisture sensor
Temperature sensor (DHT11/22)
Light sensor (LDR)
16x2 I2C LCD / 0.96" OLED
Start here
Begin by testing each sensor on the Serial monitor, then add the display, alerts, calibration, and finally a pump if desired. Prepare a README and a short 10-minute overview video for presentation and grading.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this capstone you will demonstrate five practical skills combined into four verified milestones. First, you will test sensors and read stable analog and digital values. That means understanding how to wire each module, how to read an LDR or moisture sensor, and how to use a DHT sensor library for temperature readings. Second, you'll integrate a display and format readable labels without flicker. Learn how to use an I2C interface or small OLED to show multiple sensor values. Third, you will implement calibration and threshold-based alerts that trigger a buzzer or LED when conditions are unsafe. This includes a user routine to set dry and wet soil references. Fourth, you'll apply non-blocking timing with millis so the system updates smoothly while still responding to alerts or pump control. Each objective links theory and practice: wiring diagrams, code organization, and documentation. After completing these objectives you should be ready to assemble an enclosure and present your design clearly. Which milestone will you record first in your README?

screens.title: Objectives — Practical outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of the capstone you will be able to wire sensors safely, write clear functions to read values, and present those values on a display with readable labels. You will also create a calibration routine that records dry and wet soil references so your alerts are meaningful for the exact sensor you used. Additionally, you'll structure code into functions and comments so graders can follow your logic, and you will assemble a short video and documentation that explains wiring, the block diagram, and grading results. Practically, these outcomes matter because sensor readings vary by device and environment. Calibration and documentation let you tune the system for a specific pot, soil type, and light setup. As a learner, aim to show working Serial outputs, a stable display, functioning alerts, and a clear README. Which of these outcomes will you highlight in your presentation?

screens.title: Project breakdown: components and roles
screens.narratorSegment: Begin with a clear definition of the parts and their roles. The Arduino Uno or a compatible board is the controller that reads sensor voltages and drives the display and outputs. The soil moisture sensor provides a raw analog reading that correlates with water content. The DHT11 or DHT22 supplies temperature and relative humidity readings through a digital protocol; note that the DHT22 offers higher accuracy but either is acceptable. The light-dependent resistor or light sensor gives a measure of ambient light useful for deciding whether a plant is in poor lighting. The 16x2 I2C LCD or a small OLED is required to show the three live values with labels and status indicators. Optional components include a relay module and small pump for automatic watering, and a buzzer or LED for audible or visible alerts. Breadboard, jumper wires, and resistors complete connections. Understanding these roles matters because each component shapes how you calibrate, sample, and protect the Arduino. A common misconception is to treat the soil sensor as precise without calibration; instead, use a simple calibration routine so thresholds are meaningful. To check your plan, list each component and explain its input or output role in one sentence.

screens.title: Sensor testing and verification routine
screens.narratorSegment: A systematic testing routine keeps integration manageable. First, power the Arduino and one sensor at a time. For the soil moisture sensor, read the analog value repeatedly and print it to Serial so you can observe stability as moisture changes. For the DHT sensor, use the recommended library and read temperature and humidity several times to allow the sensor to stabilize, since initial readings may be noisy. For the LDR, read the analog value while changing light levels to see the range. Always record a small sample set so you can choose calibration points later. A common mistake is to skip averaging: single reads can vary. Use a short rolling average or take multiple readings and compute the mean before deciding that a value is stable. After individual tests, verify that each sensor works while the others are connected, because wiring noise or power draw can change readings. Practical example: test the soil sensor in dry potting soil, then in damp soil, and note the two reference values. This process ensures your thresholds will be meaningful and reproducible. Sensor testing and verification routine means verify each sensor alone and record representative readings for calibration to avoid false alerts after integration.. In practical terms, a step-by-step approach to isolate and verify each input. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Sensor testing routine
Step-by-step test sequence
1. Single-sensor power-up
Connect only the sensor and check Serial for stable outputs before adding other modules.
2. Collect sample readings
Record multiple values in dry and wet or dim and bright conditions to choose calibration points.
3. Average and smooth
Compute a simple average of several reads to reduce noise before displaying or comparing to thresholds.
4. Full-system check
Reconnect all sensors, then verify that individual readings remain consistent with earlier samples.
Concrete example
Measure soil analog value in an empty pot (dry) and with a known wet sample. Record five reads each, compute the mean, and store those as your dry and wet calibration references. Use those to calculate a normalized moisture percentage in code.
Common mistake

Using a single instantaneous read as a threshold can produce false alerts. Average samples and retest after wiring all modules.

screens.title: Display integration and formatting
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating a small I2C LCD or OLED is about reliable updates and readable labels. Start by initializing the display library in setup so the screen is ready before loop runs. Format each line with short labels like Moist:, Temp:, Light: and include units so viewers can interpret values quickly. To avoid flicker, update the display at a controlled cadence and only write characters that have changed, or use a buffered update method offered by many OLED libraries. If you test on a 16x2 LCD, prioritize the most important two fields on the first line and cycle secondary information only when needed. A common misconception is that faster screen refresh is always better; excessive redraws can cause visible flicker and use processing time better spent reading sensors. A concrete example: compute a smoothed moisture percentage and refresh the display every 500 to 1000 milliseconds while sensor reads occur more frequently if needed. Finally, include clear labels and consider extra characters or icons to indicate alert states so a user can read status at a glance. Display integration and formatting means initialize the display once, format concise labels, and update the screen at a controlled cadence to avoid flicker and keep the ui legible.. In practical terms, show multiple values clearly without flicker. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Calibration routine for soil moisture
screens.narratorSegment: Calibration makes soil moisture readings comparable across sensors and soil types. A recommended routine prompts the user to place the sensor in a dry potting mix and record multiple analog samples, computing an average to define the dry reference. Next, place the sensor in thoroughly wet soil or a known wet medium and record several samples to establish the wet reference. From those two references you can map an analog value into a percentage or normalized scale. This lets you trigger alerts relative to the plant's actual requirements rather than an arbitrary number. For user experience, provide a simple two-step calibration mode activated once during setup or via a short button press, and store the resulting values in non-volatile memory if available so they persist after power cycles. A common misconception is that factory defaults work for every pot; they do not. Document the calibration steps in the README and show both raw and normalized values in your testing notes so graders can reproduce your thresholds. Calibration routine for soil moisture means use dry and wet reference readings to normalize analog moisture readings and produce reliable thresholds.. In practical terms, set dry and wet reference values so alerts are meaningful. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Calibration = meaningful alerts
keyIdea.text: Use dry and wet reference readings to normalize analog moisture readings and produce reliable thresholds.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Calibration Routine
Calibration steps
  1. Record 5–10 analog samples in dry soil; compute the mean as dryRef.
  2. Record 5–10 samples in wet soil; compute the mean as wetRef.
  3. Map current analogValue using those refs to a 0–100 scale for display.
  4. Save refs in EEPROM or note them in README if non-volatile storage isn't used.
Example mapping
Normalized percent = (analog - dryRef) / (wetRef - dryRef) * 100. Clamp to 0–100 and use this value to decide alerts. Keep the raw references in documentation so others can reproduce your thresholds.
Pro tip

Take samples at different depths and average if your sensor placement varies. Note the exact pot and soil in your README.

screens.title: Alerts, thresholds, and user feedback
screens.narratorSegment: Alerts translate sensor data into actionable feedback. Define thresholds relative to your calibrated moisture percentage and ambient light values so alerts represent meaningful conditions for the plant. Use a visible LED for simple indication, or a buzzer for audible warnings when moisture is below the dry threshold or light is persistently low. Keep alerts discriminating: avoid toggling frequently by including hysteresis or a small time delay so the alert requires the condition to persist for several seconds before triggering. This reduces false positives from transient noise. A common misconception is that an immediate alert is always best; in practice, users appreciate stable alerts that reflect sustained conditions. On the display, add a short status label like "OK", "DRY", or "LOW LIGHT" and consider a small icon change to draw attention. When you include a pump, only activate it for a short, documented duration and require a clear safety separation of pump power from the Arduino to avoid backflow of current. Ask yourself: how will a user know whether the system alerted correctly and what action to take? Alerts, thresholds, and user feedback means use calibrated thresholds, hysteresis, and short delays to produce reliable alerts; display status labels and document pump safety if used.. In practical terms, designing clear signals when the plant needs attention. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Alerts & Thresholds
Alert design patterns
  • Use calibrated percent values for moisture thresholds.
  • Add hysteresis or a short persistence timer so alerts only occur for sustained conditions.
  • Present clear text states on the display: OK, DRY, LOW LIGHT.
  • For actuators, document safety power separation and limit pump on-time to a few seconds.
Example scenario
If moisture percent drops below the calibrated dry threshold and stays below for ten seconds, light an LED and show "DRY". If pump control is enabled, run the pump for a short, documented burst and then wait a cooldown period before allowing another automatic cycle.
Common mistake

Triggering alerts on every small fluctuation will frustrate users and reduce trust in the system. Use persistence checks to avoid this.

screens.title: Optional pump control and relay safety
screens.narratorSegment: Adding a pump requires attention to power and safety. A relay module can switch a separate pump supply, keeping the Arduino's power lines independent from the pump's higher current. Always power the pump from an appropriate external source and switch its ground and positive lines through the relay as recommended by the relay manufacturer. Use a transistor or opto-isolation if you choose direct transistor switching instead of a relay. Include diodes or flyback protection when controlling inductive loads. In software, require a deliberate condition and a short, limited run time before turning the pump off, and implement a cooldown so the pump doesn't cycle too often. A common misconception is that the Arduino can power the pump directly; in nearly all cases this is unsafe. Document your wiring clearly and include a safety note in the README that lists the pump voltage, current, and the relay rating. For grading, show that the relay isolates the Arduino and that the pump runs only under calibrated and documented conditions. Optional pump control and relay safety means always power pumps from a separate supply and switch them with a relay or proper transistor driver; document ratings and safety measures.. In practical terms, how to add an actuator without risking the arduino. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.4 › Pump Control & Safety
Architecture snapshot
Controller (Arduino) sends a control signal to a relay module. The relay switches the pump's external power. Keep the pump's supply separate and document voltage and current. Use limited run times and cooldowns in software to avoid overwatering.
Checklist
  • Use a separate power supply for the pump and document its specs.
  • Switch the pump using a relay or dedicated driver, not the Arduino pin directly.
  • Limit pump activation time and add a cooldown interval in code.
  • Include wiring diagrams and safety notes in your README for assessment.

screens.title: Non-blocking timing with millis()
screens.narratorSegment: Non-blocking timing keeps your system responsive. The core idea is to record a timestamp using millis and compare the elapsed time to a desired interval instead of pausing execution with delays. For example, sample sensors every 200 milliseconds while refreshing the display every 500 to 1000 milliseconds and checking alert persistence on a separate timer. This allows the device to respond to button presses or to manage pump cycles without freezing sensor updates. A typical misconception is that using delay is acceptable for simple projects; delay blocks the microcontroller, preventing other tasks from running. With millis you can manage multiple independent timers: read sensors frequently, accumulate samples for smoothing, update the display at a human-friendly cadence, and enforce pump cooldowns after actuation. When designing code, separate responsibilities into functions: readSensors, updateDisplay, checkAlerts, controlPump. This keeps your loop organized and easy to test. A helpful check is to simulate a long pump run: with millis-based timing the display and sensors continue to update, maintaining system transparency and reliability. Non-blocking timing with millis() means use millis to manage independent timers so the system continues sensing and displaying while alerts or pump actions run.. In practical terms, keep sensor reads and alerts responsive without delay(). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. narration.text: Non-blocking timing keeps your system responsive. The core idea is to record a timestamp using millis and compare the elapsed time to a desired interval instead of pausing execution with delays. This allows the device to respond to button presses or to manage pump cycles without freezing sensor updates. A typical misconception is that using delay is acceptable for simple projects; delay blocks the microcontroller, preventing other tasks from running. With millis you can manage multiple independent timers: read sensors frequently, accumulate samples for smoothing, update the display at a human-friendly cadence, and enforce pump cooldowns after actuation. When designing code, separate responsibilities into functions: readSensors, updateDisplay, checkAlerts, controlPump. This keeps your loop organized and easy to test. A helpful check is to simulate a long pump run: with millis-based timing the display and sensors continue to update, maintaining system transparency and reliability. Timing pattern
now = millis()

Design tips

Using delay for timing will pause all tasks and make your display and alerts unresponsive during long actions like pump runs.

fullNarratorScript:
This capstone brief frames a practical, end-to-end project: a Smart Plant Monitoring System. You will plan and assemble sensors that measure soil moisture, light, and temperature, present their readings on a small I2C display, and create alerts when the plant needs attention. The project is deliberately modular. That means you first validate each sensor, then integrate the display, then add alerts and calibration, and finally optionally add a relay-driven pump. In practice, this structure helps isolate problems and keeps your code organized. A clear wiring diagram and a README are required for assessment, so document as you go. Throughout, use non-blocking timing with the millis function so your device remains responsive while updating sensors and alarms. Think of this capstone as a demonstration of skills from earlier modules: wiring, analog reading, I2C, conditional logic, debouncing ideas, and safe actuator control. As you build, record a short overview video walking through your block diagram, wiring, expected code structure, and grading criteria. That video tells the story of your design choices. Before you start, ask: which part will you test first, and how will you verify reliable sensor readings?

In this capstone you will demonstrate five practical skills combined into four verified milestones. First, you will test sensors and read stable analog and digital values. That means understanding how to wire each module, how to read an LDR or moisture sensor, and how to use a DHT sensor library for temperature readings. Second, you'll integrate a display and format readable labels without flicker. Learn how to use an I2C interface or small OLED to show multiple sensor values. Third, you will implement calibration and threshold-based alerts that trigger a buzzer or LED when conditions are unsafe. This includes a user routine to set dry and wet soil references. Fourth, you'll apply non-blocking timing with millis so the system updates smoothly while still responding to alerts or pump control. Each objective links theory and practice: wiring diagrams, code organization, and documentation. After completing these objectives you should be ready to assemble an enclosure and present your design clearly. Which milestone will you record first in your README?

By the end of the capstone you will be able to wire sensors safely, write clear functions to read values, and present those values on a display with readable labels. You will also create a calibration routine that records dry and wet soil references so your alerts are meaningful for the exact sensor you used. Additionally, you'll structure code into functions and comments so graders can follow your logic, and you will assemble a short video and documentation that explains wiring, the block diagram, and grading results. Practically, these outcomes matter because sensor readings vary by device and environment. Calibration and documentation let you tune the system for a specific pot, soil type, and light setup. As a learner, aim to show working Serial outputs, a stable display, functioning alerts, and a clear README. Which of these outcomes will you highlight in your presentation?

Begin with a clear definition of the parts and their roles. The Arduino Uno or a compatible board is the controller that reads sensor voltages and drives the display and outputs. The soil moisture sensor provides a raw analog reading that correlates with water content. The DHT11 or DHT22 supplies temperature and relative humidity readings through a digital protocol; note that the DHT22 offers higher accuracy but either is acceptable. The light-dependent resistor or light sensor gives a measure of ambient light useful for deciding whether a plant is in poor lighting. The 16x2 I2C LCD or a small OLED is required to show the three live values with labels and status indicators. Optional components include a relay module and small pump for automatic watering, and a buzzer or LED for audible or visible alerts. Breadboard, jumper wires, and resistors complete connections. Understanding these roles matters because each component shapes how you calibrate, sample, and protect the Arduino. A common misconception is to treat the soil sensor as precise without calibration; instead, use a simple calibration routine so thresholds are meaningful. To check your plan, list each component and explain its input or output role in one sentence.

A systematic testing routine keeps integration manageable. First, power the Arduino and one sensor at a time. For the soil moisture sensor, read the analog value repeatedly and print it to Serial so you can observe stability as moisture changes. For the DHT sensor, use the recommended library and read temperature and humidity several times to allow the sensor to stabilize, since initial readings may be noisy. For the LDR, read the analog value while changing light levels to see the range. Always record a small sample set so you can choose calibration points later. A common mistake is to skip averaging: single reads can vary. Use a short rolling average or take multiple readings and compute the mean before deciding that a value is stable. After individual tests, verify that each sensor works while the others are connected, because wiring noise or power draw can change readings. Practical example: test the soil sensor in dry potting soil, then in damp soil, and note the two reference values. This process ensures your thresholds will be meaningful and reproducible. Format each line with short labels like Moist:, Temp:, Light: and include units so viewers can interpret values quickly.
